attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, presented as his view.

semantics.note: Keeps the hedged canary part ('likely', not scored) apart from the firm conditional ('will dramatically slow'). Keeps the antecedent and 'both'. Only the conditional is scoreable, and only if its antecedent occurs.

contract.note: Fair, ordinary reading. It requires the profitability antecedent across both customers and providers, and it requires order data rather than revenue. 'Meaningful profits' and 'dramatically slow' have no thresholds, so the reading decides the result.

evidence.note: Nvidia 10-Q for the quarter ending July 2026, available before the cutoff. It reports revenue growth, not orders, and says nothing about the profitability antecedent.
Vendor survey from 2025 on margin pressure among software producers. It does not show a failure to make meaningful profits across customers and providers.

reviews.rationale: Firm conditional forecast with no deadline. Nothing in the packet shows that the antecedent (AI failing to drive meaningful profits for both customers and providers) has happened, and there is no series of order data. Revenue growth is context only. The canary clause is hedged and not scored. The antecedent is unknown and no conclusive event exists, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'There is no iPhone moment coming' is a firm, unbounded negative forecast. 'I'm afraid' expresses regret, not doubt. No deadline is stated.

contract.note: An ordinary reading: a breakthrough after the post, with sustained mass adoption and a durable change in everyday use. 'iPhone moment' has no threshold, so whether current adoption qualifies turns on the reading.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure: 700M weekly users and everyday task use by mid-2025. Partial counterevidence on adoption. As a company source about itself, it alone cannot meet the contradiction rule.
Independent Pew survey, Feb 2026: about a quarter of US adults use chatbots daily, but half don't use them at all. Partial counterevidence; it does not show a transformation comparable to the iPhone.
Pew browsing data: fewer clicks on links when an AI summary appears. Partial evidence of changed search behaviour; observational, and limited to one setting.

reviews.rationale: Unbounded forecast. It cannot be supported just because the event hasn't happened. The contradiction rule needs both sustained mass adoption and a durable, broad change in everyday technology use after April 2024. The packet shows substantial adoption and some change in behaviour, but not clearly a qualifying breakthrough. Without a conclusive event, the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Restates the general 'hallmark' remark and the hedged impression of coverage ('never seem to'). The context implies the AI industry is high-revenue and negative-profit, but the words don't say so outright, so leaving that out is defensible.

contract.note: Rightly treats 'hallmark' as a warning sign, not a test, and 'never seem' as a hedged impression of an undefined set of 'glossy stories'. It is fair not to score this as a literal universal claim.

evidence.note: August 2023 article on revenue that also mentions losses, which goes against a literal reading. A November 2024 update leaves its pre-post wording uncertain. One article, not a sample.
January 2024 article on revenue that does discuss profitability for both companies. One counterexample, which cannot settle a hedged impression of coverage in general.

reviews.rationale: The bubble 'hallmark' is a general heuristic that cannot be tested. The coverage remark is a hedged impression ('never seem to') about an undefined set of 'glossy stories', with no sample or threshold. The counterexamples challenge only a literal universal reading. No fair binary test exists.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the subject (smaller models trained on limited synthetic data) and the 'in many cases' scope. It is a firm causal claim that a proposed remedy doesn't work. 'Broken tool' is partly rhetorical.

contract.note: The reading is fair and ordinary. But neither 'running out' nor 'fix the overall problem' has a threshold, and 'data' could mean several things, so I think interpretation does affect the result, unlike the contract's 'false'.

evidence.note: Epoch analysis from June 2024: if trends continue, demand reaches the stock of public human text between 2026 and 2032; evidence on synthetic data is mixed. A projection, not an observed binding shortage, and it does not show synthetic data fails.
Microsoft's own description of how Phi-2 was trained, with synthetic data plus filtered web data. It documents the small-model approach but does not show it solves data scarcity across the industry.

April 2024 preprint: accumulating synthetic data alongside real data avoids collapse in the tested settings. This weakens the 'broken tool' mechanism but doesn't show the aggregate constraint is removed.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows a projected constraint on public human text and mixed evidence on synthetic data. Collapse can be mitigated when data accumulate. Nothing establishes that a binding shortage exists, or that limited synthetic-data methods either fail to remove or do remove the aggregate constraint. How common the practice is ('many cases') is not measured either. The evidence does not settle the causal claim.
